problem.title: Design a Global Anycast L4/L7 Edge Load Balancer with DSR & Zero-Drop PoP Drain
problem.tagline: Handling 20 Tbps global ingress across 30+ PoPs with XDP Maglev L4, Direct Server Return, and <3s PoP failover.
problem.purpose: Design a planetary-scale L4/L7 edge load balancing fabric that absorbs DDoS spikes, avoids L4 egress bottlenecks via Direct Server Return, and drains unhealthy PoPs without resetting active user streams.
problem.prompt: Design a global edge load balancer across 30 PoPs handling 20 Tbps egress / 50M RPS (90% HTTPS/QUIC, 10% WebSockets), with <3s automated unhealthy-PoP withdrawal and zero TCP RSTs during L4/L7 autoscaling.

prerequisites.title: BGP Anycast & Maglev ECMP
prerequisites.summary: Understand `/24` Anycast routing and why Maglev's 65,537-slot lookup table prevents ECMP reshuffling.

prerequisites.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
prerequisites.summary: Know why asymmetric return paths (L7 proxy -> client directly) save 80–90% of L4 balancer NIC bandwidth.

spark.summary: Use BGP Anycast across 30 PoPs, eBPF/XDP Maglev L4 balancers with GRE/IPIP Direct Server Return to Envoy L7 proxies, and graceful BGP drain + QUIC CID migration.
spark.keyTakeaway: When designing a multi-Tbps global edge load balancer, offload return traffic from L4 via Direct Server Return and pair Maglev ECMP with BGP graceful-shutdown + QUIC Connection IDs so PoP drains never drop active streams.
spark.byteSummary:
At 20 Tbps global egress (video, APIs, static assets), ingress requests are tiny (1–2 KB) while responses are 10x–50x larger. If your L4 load balancers proxy both directions, you need 10x as many L4 machines just to push return packets out of their NICs.

The architecture splits into three layers: (1) Global BGP Anycast across 30 PoPs announces shared `/24` prefixes so traffic enters the nearest PoP at L3; (2) Inside each PoP, eBPF/XDP Maglev L4 balancers run O(1) consistent hashing + local conntrack and encapsulate ingress packets in IPIP/GRE to Envoy L7 proxies; (3) Envoy strips the tunnel, terminates TLS/HTTP/3, and replies directly to the client using Direct Server Return (DSR) with the Anycast VIP on its loopback—completely bypassing L4 on egress.

To drain a PoP in <3 seconds without killing active flows, an edge health daemon withdraws BGP routes (or prepends AS-path for planned maintenance) while QUIC Connection IDs encode the origin PoP so any packets rerouted to a neighboring PoP are tunneled back to the active session.

learningJourney.title: R & E · Requirements, Asymmetric Bandwidth & DSR Math
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Quantifies why Direct Server Return (DSR) cuts L4 infrastructure cost by ~10x.

explanation.foundation: HTTP traffic is heavily asymmetric: a 500-byte `GET` request triggers a 50 KB JSON or media response (a 100:1 egress-to-ingress ratio, ~10:1–20:1 on average across mixed API traffic).
explanation.core: Illustrative Sizing: Across 30 PoPs, 20 Tbps egress averages ~667 Gbps/PoP (bursting to 2 Tbps/PoP), while ingress is only ~1–2 Tbps globally (~33–67 Gbps/PoP). With DSR, L4 balancers only handle 67 Gbps ingress per PoP (2x 100GbE NICs per L4 box, 2–4 boxes/PoP) instead of 2 Tbps egress!
explanation.deepDive: Using eBPF/XDP at the NIC driver layer, each L4 node forwards ~10–14 Mpps/core before the Linux sk_buff allocator even runs—keeping L4 forwarding latency under 50 microseconds.

learningJourney.title: S · State & Conntrack Tables in eBPF Maps
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Defines the exact per-CPU eBPF map layout for zero-lock Maglev + conntrack forwarding.

explanation.foundation: Software L4 balancers cannot acquire global mutexes at 10 Mpps; all state must live in lock-free per-CPU eBPF maps.
explanation.core: Each L4 node maintains: (1) `maglev_table` (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY`, 65,537 entries -> Envoy VIP index); (2) `conntrack_lru` (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_LRU_PERCPU_HASH`, 4M entries keyed by 5-tuple -> `{backend_ip, last_seen_ns}`); (3) `vip_backends` (`BPF_MAP_TYPE_ARRAY` of healthy Envoy IPs + weights).
explanation.deepDive: When Envoy health checks fail, the control plane updates `maglev_table` atomically via map-in-map swap in <1 ms—zero packet drops and zero lock contention on the XDP data plane.

learningJourney.title: H & A · Global Anycast + L4/L7 + DSR Packet Flow
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Traces a packet end-to-end from user device through Anycast, Maglev, Envoy, and DSR return.

explanation.foundation: A user sends a packet to Anycast VIP `198.51.100.1`. BGP routes it to the closest PoP's border routers, which ECMP-hash the 5-tuple to one of the PoP's Maglev L4 servers.
explanation.core: Maglev checks `conntrack_lru` (or `maglev_table` on SYN), wraps the packet in an IPIP/GRE header addressed to the chosen Envoy L7 node's unicast IP, and transmits it. Envoy decapsulates the packet—revealing the original `(client_ip -> 198.51.100.1)`—terminates TLS/HTTP, and sends the response straight out the PoP gateway with source IP `198.51.100.1`.
explanation.deepDive: Note on ISP anti-spoofing (uRPF): Envoy must have `198.51.100.1/32` bound on its `lo` interface (with `arp_ignore=1`) and the PoP's ToR/border routers must allow outbound packets from `198.51.100.1` without dropping them as spoofed.

learningJourney.title: D · Detailed Design: <3s PoP Drain & QUIC CID Migration
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Prevents blackholing during PoP outages and keeps active sessions alive during BGP shifts.

explanation.foundation: If a PoP loses upstream transit or Envoy health checks drop below threshold, its BGP daemon (ExaBGP / BIRD / GoBGP) must withdraw the Anycast prefix fast.
explanation.core: With BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) + 500 ms local health probes, an unhealthy PoP withdraws its BGP announcement in <2 seconds. For active QUIC/HTTP3 connections, the 8-byte QUIC Connection ID encodes `(pop_id, server_id)`: if BGP shifts a user to PoP 2 mid-stream, PoP 2 reads `pop_id=1` from the CID and tunnels those packets over the private backbone to PoP 1.
explanation.deepDive: For planned maintenance, the BGP daemon first attaches the `GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN` community (`65535:0`) and prepends its AS-path 3x so new connections move to neighboring PoPs while existing TCP/WebSocket connections finish draining over 60 seconds.

codeExample.title: Automated BGP Anycast Health-Check & Graceful Drain Controller
codeExample.code:
def evaluate_pop_health(envoy_ready_ratio, packet_drop_pct, bgp_client, draining=False):
    prefix = '198.51.100.0/24'
    if draining:
        # Planned maintenance: prepend AS-path + graceful-shutdown community
        bgp_client.announce(prefix, communities=['65535:0'], prepend=3)
        return 'DRAINING'
    if envoy_ready_ratio < 0.50 or packet_drop_pct > 2.0:
        # Unhealthy PoP: withdraw immediately (<3s failover via BFD/BGP)
        bgp_client.withdraw(prefix)
        return 'WITHDRAWN'
    bgp_client.announce(prefix, communities=[], prepend=0)
    return 'HEALTHY'

decisionFramework.problem: How to drain or fail over an Anycast PoP without dropping active sessions or blackholing traffic.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Kill the BGP speaker process abruptly on maintenance or rely on 60s BGP hold timers.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: 60s hold timers blackhole traffic for a full minute; abrupt withdrawal resets every active TCP connection in flight.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Abrupt BGP kill vs. BFD + Graceful-Shutdown Community + QUIC CID Backbone Tunneling.
decisionFramework.decision: Use BFD (<2s hard-failure withdrawal), BGP `65535:0` graceful drain for maintenance, and QUIC CID routing for mid-stream PoP shifts.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Requires private inter-PoP backbone capacity for tunneled QUIC flows and strict uRPF/DSR router config.

decisionExercise.prompt: During a PoP's peak 1.5 Tbps video-streaming burst, Envoy L7 proxies are healthy, but your Maglev L4 servers hit 100% NIC TX saturation. What architectural change removes the bottleneck?

options.label: Enable Direct Server Return (DSR) with IPIP/GRE encapsulation so Envoy L7 replies directly to clients without passing back through Maglev L4.
options.explanation: Correct! DSR removes 90%+ of egress bandwidth from L4 balancers, cutting L4 NIC load to ingress-only (~50–100 Gbps).

options.label: Switch Maglev from 65,537 slots to 100 slots.
options.explanation: Smaller Maglev tables worsen load skew and do not reduce total egress bytes.

options.label: Disable TCP connection tracking on L4.
options.explanation: Disabling conntrack breaks active TCP flows on scale-out without reducing egress traffic.

learningJourney.title: E & D · Evaluation, Assumptions, Limitations & Glossary
learningJourney.whyThisMatters: Documents network assumptions, DSR limitations, and key edge-routing terminology.

explanation.foundation: DSR requires L2/L3 adjacency (or IPIP/GRE support) between L4 balancers and L7 proxies and permissive uRPF on egress border routers.
explanation.core: Assumptions & Limitations: Bandwidth estimates assume 10:1–20:1 egress-to-ingress asymmetry across 30 PoPs, an owned ASN with `/24` IPv4 / `/48` IPv6 prefixes, and private backbone tunnels for QUIC CID migration. In public cloud VPCs where raw source-IP spoofing (DSR) is blocked by SDN hypervisors, you must use cloud-native GWLB (GENEVE) or symmetric L4 proxies.
explanation.deepDive: Glossary: DSR (Direct Server Return — L7 replies directly to client bypassing L4); XDP (eXpress Data Path — in-kernel NIC-driver packet processing); BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection — sub-second link failure protocol); uRPF (Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding — anti-spoofing check that must allow Anycast VIP egress).

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does Direct Server Return (DSR) dramatically reduce L4 load balancer hardware requirements at a 20 Tbps edge?

options.text: DSR lets L7 proxies reply directly to clients, keeping 90%+ of asymmetric egress traffic off L4 balancer NICs.
options.feedback: Correct! L4 balancers only process small ingress requests while L7 handles heavy egress directly.
DSR is an asymmetric L3/L4 routing pattern, not compression.
DSR works together with BGP Anycast.

options.text: DSR moves TLS termination onto the client browser.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Asymmetric web/video traffic has 10x–20x more egress than ingress; DSR keeps egress off L4.

knowledgeChecks.question: What network check on edge/ToR routers can silently drop Direct Server Return (DSR) egress packets from Envoy L7?

options.text: Strict Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) rejecting outbound packets sourced from the Anycast VIP.
options.feedback: Correct! Border routers must use loose uRPF or explicit VIP allowlists so DSR return traffic is not flagged as spoofed.
DNSSEC runs on DNS, not HTTPS egress.
Maglev tables have fixed size M.
HPACK is an L7 protocol feature.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Strict uRPF checks if the source IP routes back out the same interface; DSR replies use the loopback VIP.

knowledgeChecks.question: How can a global Anycast edge preserve an active QUIC connection if a BGP route flap shifts the client from PoP 1 to PoP 2 mid-stream?

options.text: Encode `(pop_id, server_id)` in the QUIC Connection ID so PoP 2 tunnels packets over the private backbone back to PoP 1.
options.feedback: Correct! Self-routing QUIC CIDs survive both client IP changes and mid-stream BGP PoP shifts.

options.text: Wait 60 seconds for GeoDNS caches to expire.
options.feedback: GeoDNS does not rescue mid-stream L3 shifts.

options.text: Broadcast every packet to all 30 PoPs simultaneously.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: QUIC Connection IDs decouple connection identity from IP/routing paths, enabling deterministic backbone forwarding.

beginner.summary: Build a global edge load balancer using BGP Anycast across 30 locations, Maglev L4 balancers, and Direct Server Return so replies skip the L4 hop.
beginner.keyTakeaway: When building a high-bandwidth global edge, use BGP Anycast for fast routing and Direct Server Return so heavy responses go straight from L7 proxies to users.
beginner.byteSummary: BGP Anycast sends users to the closest PoP, Maglev L4 forwards requests to Envoy L7, and Envoy sends big responses straight back to the user (DSR) so L4 never gets overloaded.

intermediate.summary: Combine 30-PoP BGP Anycast, eBPF/XDP Maglev L4 + conntrack, IPIP/GRE DSR to Envoy L7, and <3s BFD/BGP withdrawal.
intermediate.keyTakeaway: When designing a 20 Tbps edge ingress, pair XDP Maglev + DSR to offload L4 egress with BFD/BGP withdrawal and QUIC CID tunneling for PoP failover.
intermediate.byteSummary: XDP Maglev handles ~1.5 Tbps ingress with O(1) consistent hashing, Envoy replies directly via DSR to offload 20 Tbps egress, and BFD + QUIC CIDs enable <3s PoP failover.

advanced.summary: Multi-Tbps planetary edge with XDP per-CPU conntrack, atomic map-in-map Maglev swaps, loose-uRPF DSR, BGP 65535:0 graceful drain, and QUIC CID backbone tunneling.
advanced.keyTakeaway: When operating stateful edge traffic across 30+ Anycast PoPs, use atomic eBPF map swaps, BGP graceful-shutdown communities, and self-routing QUIC CIDs.
advanced.byteSummary: Lock-free per-CPU eBPF conntrack + 65,537-slot Maglev maps scale to 10+ Mpps/core, while DSR (with loose uRPF), BFD <3s withdrawal, and QUIC CID tunneling preserve active streams through PoP drains and BGP flaps.
